name: Mantra repetition (japa)
method_summary: The repetition of a mantra received from a teacher — a seed syllable, the praṇava, a divine name, a Vedic verse or a longer formula — with attention to its sound and meaning. Before repetition the practitioner states the mantra's seer, metre and deity (viniyoga) and places its parts on the body (nyāsa); the count is kept on a rosary (akṣamālā) or the finger-joints. It is done aloud (vācika), whispered (upāṃśu) or mentally (mānasa), each far superior to the previous; Patañjali joins repetition to contemplation of its meaning (YS 1.28). A course of fixed counts with supplementary rites (puraścaraṇa) 'masters' a mantra for use.
prerequisites: a mantra received from a qualified guru (for Āgamic mantras)
purity, a fixed seat and time
signs_of_progress: the inward consciousness is realized and obstacles vanish (YS 1.29)
the deity, praised by japa, is pleased and gives enjoyment and liberation (Padmanābhīya quoted in the Padārthādarśa)

warnings.text: A mantra wrong in tone or letter does not convey the meaning intended; as a verbal thunderbolt it harms the sacrificer.
Mantras with defects such as being 'cut' do not protect the practitioner; they must first be purified.
The mantra being repeated is to be kept secret (gopana).
In mental japa one should not move head, neck, tongue or lips.

equivalents.note: U04's entry for the three kinds of japa
U02's entry (Manusmṛti) for the three kinds
repetition of the divine name as the mantra
the 'unrepeated' haṃsa mantra of the breath

name: Spoken (audible) repetition — vācika japa
method_summary: Uttering the mantra aloud with its proper high, low and circumflex tones and clear words and syllables; ten times better than ritual sacrifice.

warnings.text: A mantra wrong in tone or letter does not convey the meaning intended; as a verbal thunderbolt it harms the sacrificer.

equivalents.note: one of the three modes

name: Whispered repetition — upāṃśu japa
method_summary: Uttering the mantra slowly, the lips moving slightly, barely audible even to oneself; a hundred times better than ritual sacrifice.

equivalents.note: one of the three modes

name: Mental repetition — mānasa japa
method_summary: Reciting inwardly, with the intellect, the series of the mantra's letters, notes and words while remembering its meaning, without moving head, tongue or lips; a thousand times better than ritual sacrifice.

warnings.text: In mental japa one should not move head, neck, tongue or lips.

equivalents.note: one of the three modes

name: Repetition of and meditation on Oṃ (praṇava-japa, praṇava-upāsanā)
method_summary: Repeating Oṃ, the designator of the Lord (YS 1.27), while contemplating its meaning (1.28); meditating on its measures a, u, m as waking, dream and deep sleep and on the measureless fourth as the self (Māṇḍūkya 8–12); fixing the mind on Oṃ as the fearless Brahman (MK 1.25); taking Oṃ as the bow, the self as the arrow and Brahman as the target (Muṇḍaka 2.2.3–4); prolonging its sound into the subtle phases beyond the three letters until it dissolves in the soundless; uttering it at death while remembering the Lord (BhG 8.13).
signs_of_progress: realization of the inward consciousness and removal of obstacles (YS 1.29)

warnings.text: The fruit depends on the measures meditated: one measure leads back to the human world, two to the world of the moon, three to Brahman (the Praśna's teaching on Oṃ).

equivalents.note: U03/U13 entry for meditation on Oṃ
U04 entry
U07 entry
Pāśupata meditation on Oṃkāra in the heart (U17)

name: Repetition of the Gāyatrī (Sāvitrī)
method_summary: At the morning, noon and evening twilights (sandhyā), after sipping water and breath-restraint, the practitioner recites Oṃ, the three utterances (bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ) and the Sāvitrī verse to Savitṛ — 'we meditate on that excellent radiance of the god Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts' (RV 3.62.10) — a fixed number of times, meditating on its seer (Viśvāmitra), metre (gāyatrī) and deity (Savitṛ) and on the Goddess Gāyatrī; it is imparted at the initiation (upanayana). The Upaniṣads meditate on its three feet as the worlds, the Vedas and the breaths and on a fourth, 'visible' foot beyond them.

equivalents.note: Upaniṣadic meditation on the Gāyatrī's feet
the sectarian 'Gāyatrīs' modelled on it

notes: Who may receive the Gāyatrī is part of dsp:women-caste-liberation.

name: Repetition of the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya (Tryambaka) mantra
method_summary: Repeating, and offering into fire with, the verse to Tryambaka — 'we worship the three-eyed one, fragrant, increaser of prosperity; like a cucumber from its stalk may I be freed from death, not from immortality' (RV 7.59.12) — for release from untimely death and disease and for liberation; in the mantra manuals it is enlarged with Oṃ and seed-syllables and given with its seer, metre, deity and meditation on the three-eyed Śiva holding the jar of nectar, and is used in rites of pacification for the sick and dying.
notes: The seed-syllable forms of the manuals (e.g. with hauṃ juṃ saḥ) are recalled with low confidence and not given here.

name: Seed-syllables of the centres and elements
method_summary: Meditating on, or softly intoning, the seed-syllable of each centre with its element — laṃ (earth, root centre), vaṃ (water, svādhiṣṭhāna), raṃ (fire, maṇipūra), yaṃ (air, anāhata), haṃ (space, viśuddhi), oṃ (ājñā) — together with its shape, colour, deity and the letters on its petals; the same seeds are used in the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) before worship, where the elements of the body are dissolved upward into their sources and a divine body is re-created.
prerequisites: initiation and instruction by a guru

warnings.text: The rousing of kuṇḍalinī through the centres is to be done by the method learned from the guru.

equivalents.note: bhūtaśuddhi uses the element seeds
duplicate id of bhūtaśuddhi

name: Placing the letters on the body (mātṛkā-nyāsa)
method_summary: The fifty letters from a to kṣa, the manifestations of śabda-brahman, are installed by touch and visualization on the parts of the body (outer nyāsa) and on the petals of the inner centres (inner nyāsa), with or without the nasal bindu, so that the body becomes made of mantra before japa and worship.

equivalents.note: one form of nyāsa

name: Placing mantras on the body (nyāsa)
method_summary: U31 contribution: in the mantra manuals every japa is preceded by ṛṣyādi-nyāsa (the seer on the head, the metre in the mouth, the deity in the heart, the seed, power and pin elsewhere), the six-limbed nyāsa of the hands and body with the six endings (namaḥ, svāhā, vaṣaṭ, huṃ, vauṣaṭ, phaṭ), and mātṛkā-nyāsa of the letters.

name: Mantra initiation (mantra-dīkṣā)
method_summary: A qualified guru gives a mantra — chosen and tested for the disciple — to a qualified disciple who has served and been tested (a year for a brāhmaṇa up to four for a śūdra, ŚT 2.153), with worship of the deity and the teaching of its viniyoga and nyāsa; the mantra is thereafter kept secret.
prerequisites: a guru with the marks of ŚT 2.141–144

warnings.text: The mantra being repeated is not to be disclosed.

equivalents.note: mantra-initiation within the wider initiation rites

name: The ten purifications of a mantra (mantra-saṃskāra)
method_summary: Summary only: a defective or newly received mantra is made effective by ten rites — generation, enlivening, striking, awakening, consecration, cleansing, strengthening, satiation, kindling and guarding (secrecy) — performed according to the teacher's tradition (ŚT 2.112–123).

warnings.text: These are to be done according to tradition (sampradāya); they are kept secret in all mantras.

name: Puraścaraṇa (the preliminary mastery of a mantra)
method_summary: U31 contribution: the mantra manuals prescribe for each mantra a count of repetitions (often reckoned by its syllables), followed by fire offerings, libations, sprinkling and feeding of brāhmaṇas in diminishing tenths, under rules of diet, place and conduct; only then is the mantra used.

name: Devotional singing of the Lord's names and deeds (kīrtana, saṅkīrtana)
method_summary: Singing the names, qualities and deeds of the Lord, alone or together, with drums and cymbals, often in call-and-response; one of the nine forms of devotion (BhP 7.5.23) and, in the Kali age, the chief means (BhP 11.5.32; 12.3.51–52). Its forms include congregational chanting of the name (nāma-saṅkīrtana), narrative singing (harikathā), rāga-based songs of the singer-saints, and temple kīrtan of the Puṣṭimārga.
signs_of_progress: the voice falters, the heart melts, one weeps, laughs, sings aloud and dances unabashed (BhP 11.14.24)

warnings.text: The name is to be sung by one humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree, giving honour to others and seeking none.

equivalents.note: the congregational chanting of the name (U16)
congregational devotional singing

name: Devotional singing (bhajana, bhajan)
method_summary: Singing devotional songs and names of the deity, usually in a group led by a lead singer, with simple rhythm instruments; in the South Indian bhajana tradition an ordered sequence of songs and names to many deities culminating in the Lord's name; in the Vārkarī tradition singing the abhaṅgas of the saints; in the Sant tradition singing the śabdas of Kabīr and others.
signs_of_progress: melting of the heart and tears (BhP 11.14.24)

name: Worship through nāda (music as spiritual practice)
method_summary: Disciplined practice of notes, rāga and rhythm, offered to the deity and attended to until the mind is absorbed in the sound: the struck nāda of music, which 'delights the world and breaks worldly existence', as an easier path than the sages' worship of the unstruck nāda; by nāda-worship the three gods are worshipped. The vīṇā-player versed in śrutis and tāla goes the way of liberation without effort.
signs_of_progress: success in song when the jīva rests on certain petals of the heart, throat and lalanā centres or in the brahmarandhra (ŚR 1.2.140–144)

equivalents.note: the yogic listening to the inner (unstruck) sound; the music treatises teach the struck sound as the easier way

name: Worship of the deities of the stage (raṅga-daivata-pūjana)
method_summary: Before a theatre is used and before performances, the gods who protect each part of the stage and the jarjara staff are worshipped with offerings (NŚ 3).

name: The preliminaries of performance (pūrvaraṅga)
method_summary: Songs and instrumental pieces, partly behind the curtain, and the benediction (nāndī) performed before the play to please the gods (NŚ 5).

name: Study of grammar as purification of speech
method_summary: Learning the Pāṇinian grammar with its commentaries so as to use only correct words (sādhu-śabda), which removes the impurities of speech, brings merit and, understood to its root, leads to the Word-principle (VP 1.11–16; Mahābhāṣya on 6.1.84).
